Dīpakalikā
------------------------------------------
The religious works that regulated the conduct of the Hindus during the ancient and the medieval period, both at the personal and at the social level, are known as the धर्मशास्त्रस्. If the गृह्यसूत्रस् and the धर्मसूत्रस् form the first stratum, the smṛtis form the second. Among the smṛtis, the Yājñavalkya Smṛti is considered only next in importance to the Manusmṛti.
These smṛtis needed explanations, amplifications and clarifications of doubts as the society grew more complicated. The commentaries written by later scholars well-versed in this field, supplied the much-needed material for this.
The Dīpakalikā is such a commentary on the Yājñavalkya Smṛti written by शूलपाणि (A. D. 1365-1445). It is a brief work but quoted as an authority by well-known later writers like रघुनन्दन. His views have been considered as rather archaic.

dīpana
(‘lighting up’)
------------------------------------------
In rituals as also in spiritual practices, mantras play a very important part. These mantras have to be received in दीक्षा or spiritual initiation from a competent गुरु or teacher.
The special class of works known as the तन्त्रस् declare that a मन्त्र has to be subjected to a purificatory process if is to be effective. This process called ‘mantra-saṁskāra’ is of ten types, of which ‘dīpana’ or ‘dīpanī’ is also one. According to one view, the बीजमन्त्र or seed-letter has to be repeated seven times with the प्रणव (Oṁ) preceding and following it. This is ‘dīpana’ for that मन्त्र. For instance, ‘Gaṁ’ is the बीजमन्त्र for गणपति. In दीपन, ‘Oṁ gam Oṁ’ has to be repeated seven times.
According to another view the दीपन has to be done with the formula ‘Oṁ ह्रीṁ śrīṁ.’ The details have to be learnt from the गुरु.

Dīpāvalī
(‘row of lighted lamps’)
------------------------------------------
Being a festival of lights, decorative illuminations and fireworks, दीपावली or दिवाली is perhaps the most popular of all the Hindu festivals, bringing joy to the young and old alike. It is celebrated very widely throughout India and among the Hindus settled abroad.
It is very difficult to trace its origin and development. According to some scholars it was already a well-known festival by the time of the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa said to be composed before A. D. 1000.
In some works it has been called as ‘Kaumudī उत्सव,’ ‘a festival in which people find delight on this earth among themselves’.
Dīpāvalī proper is of three days’ duration; and with the addition of dvitīyā, it is spread over four days. It normally falls during the last part of October and the early part of November. The first day, Āśvayuja कृष्ण caturdaśī, is called ‘Narakacaturdaśī’. Originally, the celebration of this day may have been aimed at escaping from नरक or हेल्ल्, by propitiating यम, the god of death and हेल्ल्. But later, it seems to have been associated with कृष्ण’s killing of the demon नरकासुर, the king of Prāgjyotiṣapura (modern Assam). On this day one is advised to take an oil-bath at dawn, pray for the destruction of one’s sins, offer तर्पण (satiation with handful of water mixed with sesame) to यम and light a lamp to नरक. After a sumptuous feast with fourteen kinds of vegetables (since the festival starts from the 14th day), rows of lamps should be lighted in the evening illuminating all parts of one’s होउसे. Temples and public places too should be illuminated in the same way. Some religious texts suggest that the day should be spent in ड़स्तिन्ग् and that ड़ोओद् can be taken only at night.
The next day, अमावास्या, is said to be the darkest day of the year. Oil-bath, worship of लक्ष्मी, the goddess of wealth and prosperity, offerings to the पितृस् or departed manes, feeding of ब्राह्मणस् and ड़स्तिन्ग् by day are the main items of the rite on this day. Lighting of lamps and general illumination should continue as on the previous day. Since this is a day specially dedicated to लक्ष्मी and since there is every chance of अलक्ष्मी (the inauspicious goddess, the opposite of लक्ष्मी) peeping in to ruin one’s prosperity, women of the town or village are asked to create a terrible noise by beating drums and winnowing baskets around midnight !
In Bengal, Kālī is worshipped on this day in clay image, instead of लक्ष्मी, throughout the night. Hence this day is named Kālīpūjā day or festival.
In other parts of India, this is traders’ day. They adore लक्ष्मी, worship their account books, open the new account books, invite friends, customers and other traders and give them ताम्बूल (betel leaf with betel nuts) and sweets.
Next day—Kārttīka śukla pratipad—is known as ‘Balipratipadā’ or ‘Bali-pāḍyamī’. It is one of the 3½ days considered as most auspicious in the Hindu almanacs. Though there is unanimity in assigning great auspiciousness to Cāndramāna युगादि and विजयदशमी, there are differences of opinion regarding the third. Some give that privilege to बलिप्रतिपदा while others do so to Akṣayyatṛtīyā. The left over day becomes the ½!
Worship of बलि (the powerful king of the असुरस् who was vanquished and pushed into the पाताल or the nether world by विष्णु as the इन्चर्नतिओन् वामन) at night, especially by the king, is the most important rite of this day. One should also keep awake the whole night spending the time in seeing religious dramas. Gifts made on this day bring inexhaustible fruits.
On all the three or four days of the दीपावली festival, the skies are rent asunder by the terrific sounds of bursting crackers. This bursting of crackers seems to be a universal practice all over the country. It may signify not only the expression of one’s joy but also the destruction of evil personified by demons like नरकासुर.
Balipratipadā is also called ‘Dyūta-pratipadā’. ‘Dyūta’ means गम्ब्लिन्ग्. There is a curious (or queer?) direction in the Brahmapurāṇa, issued to those observing this day, to gamble! It seems that on this day पार्वती defeated शङ्कर in a game of dice and that she became very happy whereas शङ्कर was distraught with sorrow. (This scene has been shown in the एल्लोर cave no. 21.) Hence those that win in the गम्ब्लिन्ग् on this day will be happy throughout the year, the opposite being the case of those that lose! This temptation naturally makes people—even today—to gamble recklessly. बलिप्रतिपदा day!">1 May be that the writers of these पुराणस् wanted the flock not to gamble for the rest of the year! This is perhaps better than our modern contrivances like ‘Courtesy Week’ wherein people think that they need not be courteous for the remaining part of the year!
Some more observances prescribed during the celebration of the बलिप्रतिपदा may now be given. They are: worship of cows and bulls, worship of the गोवर्धन hill, tying of Mārgapālī and ārati to menfolk by the womenfolk of the family.
Cows and bulls should be decorated, worshipped and fed well. Cows must not be milked that day and bulls must not be made to work. Obviously this is a way of expressing one’s gratitude to those animals which do so much for us.
Next is the worship of the Govar-dhana hill. The ‘hill’ is prepared either out of cow-dung or out of अन्न (cooked rice) and other cooked ड़ोओद्. This latter, as also its worship, is called ‘Annakūṭa’. An image or a picture of Bālagopāla (boy कृष्ण) is also kept with it and worship is offered with 16 उपचारस्. The mantras used expressly refer to the protection that Bālakṛṣṇa gave to the people by lifting up the गोवर्धन hill and sheltering them beneath it.
Mārgapālī (‘protectress of the road’) is a rope of कुश grass and is tied to a pole on one side and a tree on the other, in the afternoon. All people including the king and the ब्राह्मणस् bow down before it and pass under it. It is perhaps the ‘goddess of the road,’ whose grace is needed to keep the town safe and also for safety during journeys. This is then followed by a tug of war between the men of the royal families and the common folk. If the common folk win, it is said to be good for the king and the country. Obviously, this is a symbolic way of expressing the simple truth that the ruler can be successful and the country well-ruled only when the people have a say in the affairs of the State.
Next comes the festival of यम-dvitīyā or Bhrātṛdvitīyā (Kārttīka śukla dvitīyā). According to an ancient legend, यम, the god of death and हेल्ल्, and the river goddess यमुना, were brother and sister. On this day of Kārttīka śukla dvitīyā, goddess यमुना is said to have invited her brother यम to her होउसे for dinner and honoured him. Hence, this day has become a day of reunion of brothers and sisters. Brothers are invited by the sisters to their houses and sumptuously fed. The former give presents to the latter. Since there is separation of the sisters after their मर्रिअगे, from their parents and brothers, and may live in far off places or may not meet for a long time, this festival provides for a much-needed opportunity for a get-together.
Sometimes, the sisters worship god यम and pray to him for the longevity of their brothers. People living on the banks of the यमुना river, do not miss taking bath in the river on this day. In some places there is a melā (fair) on the banks of the river.
See also BALIPRATIPADĀ and BHRĀTṚ-DVITĪYĀ.

dīpastambha
(‘the lamp-post’)
------------------------------------------
One of the constituents of a temple complex is the दीपस्तम्भ or the lamp-post. It is situated either in front of the बलिपीठ (pedestal of sacrificial offerings) or outside the main gate. The top of this post has a bud-shaped chamber to receive the lamp.
During the days when electricity was unknown, a lamp-post served to give some general light in the area to allow free movement.
